wordings.text: In an interview you are asked to design a URL shortener. What should come first?
options: Ask which features are needed and at what scale: custom links, expiry, reads and writes per second
Choose the database
Draw the services and how they connect
Write the function that shortens a URL

questions.explanation:
The requirements decide the design: a hundred links a day and a billion a day need
different systems. Agreeing on features and numbers first also shows the interviewer
how you approach an open problem.

wordings.text: 10 million users a day each make 20 requests. About how many requests per second is that on average?
options: About 2,300
About 230
About 23,000
About 200,000

questions.explanation:
200 million requests over 86,400 seconds is about 2,300 a second. Rounding a day to
100,000 seconds makes this quick: 200 million / 100,000 = 2,000. Peaks are often two to
three times the average.

wordings.text: A service stores 1 million new records a day, 1 KB each, and keeps them for 5 years. About how much storage does it need, before replication?
options: About 2 TB
About 200 GB
About 20 TB
About 2 PB

questions.explanation:
1 million × 1 KB = 1 GB a day; × 365 × 5 ≈ 1,800 GB, about 2 TB. Copies for replication
and backups multiply it.

wordings.text: Which of these HTTP requests are idempotent, so that sending one twice has the same effect as sending it once? Choose all that apply.
options: `GET /orders/42`
`PUT /orders/42` with the whole order
`DELETE /orders/42`
`POST /orders` with a new order

questions.explanation:
GET changes nothing, PUT sets the order to the same value again, and a second DELETE
finds nothing left to delete. Each POST creates another order, so retrying it can create
duplicates.

wordings.text: A phone app sends `POST /payments`, the connection times out, and the app sends it again. How can the server avoid charging twice?
options: The app sends a unique key with each payment; the server stores the result per key and returns it for a repeat
The app never retries a payment
The server rejects two payments of the same amount within a minute
The server makes the timeout longer

questions.explanation:
An idempotency key makes a request safe to retry: the server sees the key again and
returns the first result instead of charging again. Never retrying loses payments when
the first request did not arrive, and two equal amounts can be real.
questions.summary: Safe retries with an idempotency key

wordings.text: A feed returns posts newest first, 20 per page, with `?offset=20`. While a user reads, new posts arrive, and the next page repeats posts already seen. Which change fixes it?
options: Pages start after the last post seen: `?after=<id of that post>`
Bigger pages
Caching each page for a minute
Returning the whole feed at once

questions.explanation:
An offset counts from the top, so every new post shifts the pages by one. A cursor names
the last item seen, so the next page starts after it whatever was added. A lookup on an
indexed key is also faster than skipping many rows.

wordings.text: A server behind a load balancer starts failing its health checks. What does the load balancer do?
options: Stops sending it requests until it passes again
Restarts it
Sends it fewer requests, in proportion to its errors
Nothing, until an operator removes it

questions.explanation:
The load balancer regularly calls each server, for example on a health address, and
sends traffic only to those that answer. Restarting or replacing servers is the job of
other tools.
questions.summary: What a load balancer does with an unhealthy server

wordings.text: Web servers keep user sessions in their own memory. Behind a load balancer, users are logged out at random. Which fix also keeps users logged in when a server goes down?
options: Keep sessions in a shared store that every server reads
Send each user to the same server every time
Add more servers
Make sessions last longer

questions.explanation:
With sessions in a shared store, the servers hold no user state, so any server can
answer any request and servers can be added or removed freely. Sending a user to the same
server works until that server goes down, and it can spread load unevenly.
questions.summary: Stateless servers behind a load balancer

wordings.text: An app reads through a cache in front of its database. A read finds nothing in the cache. What happens next?
options: The app reads the database, puts the value in the cache and returns it
The app returns an error
The app returns an empty value and fills the cache later
The cache reloads the whole database

questions.explanation:
This is cache-aside: the cache holds only what has been read, and a miss costs one
database read. The next reads of the same key are served from the cache until the entry
expires or is removed.
questions.summary: A read miss in a cache-aside cache

wordings.text: Product prices are cached for an hour, and after a price change users still see the old price. Which changes help? Choose all that apply.
options: Remove or update the cached price when the price changes
Cache prices for a shorter time
Add more cache servers
Cache prices for a day

questions.explanation:
Removing the entry on change keeps the cache current; a shorter expiry limits how long a
stale value can live, at the cost of more database reads. More cache servers hold the
same stale values.

wordings.text: A very popular cache entry expires, and thousands of requests miss it at once and all query the database. Which fix stops this?
options: Let one request rebuild the entry while the others wait or get the old value
Remove the cache
Make entries expire sooner
Retry failed database queries at once

questions.explanation:
This is a cache stampede. A lock per key, or serving the old value while one request
refreshes it, turns thousands of identical queries into one. Expiring sooner makes it
happen more often.

wordings.text: A chat app splits its messages across database shards. Reads fetch one user's messages. Which shard key spreads the load and keeps such a read on one shard?
options: A hash of the user id
The date of the message
The first letter of the user name
The user's country

questions.explanation:
Hashing the user id spreads users evenly and keeps each user's messages together. By
date, all new messages go to one shard; first letters and countries are unevenly
common, so some shards get far more load.

wordings.text: Keys are spread over N servers. Why use consistent hashing instead of `hash(key) mod N`?
options: Adding or removing a server moves only about 1/N of the keys, not nearly all of them
It computes hashes faster
It needs no hash function
Every key is stored on every server

questions.explanation:
With mod N, changing N changes the server of almost every key, so a cache loses nearly
everything. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring; a new server takes
over only the keys next to it.

wordings.text: A read-heavy app sends writes to a primary database and reads to replicas that copy it. What must the app now handle?
options: A read right after a write may return the old value
Writes may go to any replica
The primary no longer needs backups
Reads become slower

questions.explanation:
Replicas copy changes after a short delay, the replication lag. Where a user must see
their own change, such as a profile they just saved, read it from the primary.

wordings.text: The CAP theorem: when a network partition splits a distributed store, it must choose between which two properties?
options: Consistency and availability
Consistency and partition tolerance
Latency and throughput
Availability and durability

questions.explanation:
During a partition, a node either refuses requests it cannot confirm, staying consistent,
or answers with data that may be out of date, staying available. Partitions happen on
real networks, so partition tolerance is not optional.
questions.summary: The trade-off of the CAP theorem

wordings.text: Which of these can be eventually consistent, briefly out of date? Choose all that apply.
options: The like count on a post
The order of posts in a news feed
The balance checked before a withdrawal
Whether a seat on a flight is still free when it is booked

questions.explanation:
A like count or a feed that is a few seconds behind harms no one. A stale balance can let
an account be overdrawn, and a stale seat can be sold twice; these need strong
consistency where the decision is made.

wordings.text: At sign-up, the welcome email is put on a queue and a separate worker sends it. What does this give? Choose all that apply.
options: The sign-up request returns sooner
Sign-up keeps working while the email service is down; the messages wait
Workers can be scaled apart from the web servers
Each email is sent exactly once

questions.explanation:
A queue decouples the request from slow or unreliable work. It does not give exactly
once: most queues deliver at least once, so a message can arrive twice after a failure.

wordings.text: A queue delivers each message at least once, so after a worker crash a message can be processed twice. How does the result stay correct?
options: Make the handler idempotent, for example by recording the ids of processed messages
Use a faster worker
Process each message twice and compare the results
Delete the message before processing it

questions.explanation:
A handler that recognises a repeat, or whose effect is the same when repeated, is safe
under at-least-once delivery. Deleting the message first loses it if the worker crashes
midway.

wordings.text: A rate limiter gives each client a bucket of up to 10 tokens, refilled at 1 token per second; each request takes a token. A client with a full bucket sends 15 requests at once. How many get through?

questions.explanation:
A full bucket allows a burst of 10; the other 5 are rejected. After that, the client can
make about one request per second, the refill rate.
questions.summary: How a token bucket limits requests

wordings.text: A service is overloaded, and its clients retry every failed call. Which changes help it recover? Choose all that apply.
options: Clients wait longer after each failure: exponential backoff
Clients add a random delay to each wait
Clients stop calling for a while after many failures: a circuit breaker
Clients retry at once, as often as needed

questions.explanation:
Immediate retries add load to a service that is already failing. Backoff spreads retries
out, randomness keeps clients from retrying all at the same moment, and a circuit breaker
gives the service time to recover.
